intro.html: Weather, moods, prices and people can all change without warning, and English has a word for each kind of change. Some describe things that swing unpredictably (erratic, volatile, fluctuate); some describe people whose moods or loyalties shift (capricious, fickle, mercurial); and some describe acting without stopping to think (impulsive, impetuous, spontaneous).

Changing moods and loyalties: capricious (on a whim), fickle (loyalty that shifts), mercurial (quick mood swings). Unpredictable things: erratic (irregular), volatile (ready to blow up), fluctuate (to rise and fall), vacillate (to waver between choices). Acting without planning: impulsive and impetuous (rash), spontaneous (natural, unplanned, often a good thing).

words.ex: The {capricious} weather switched from sunshine to hail three times in one afternoon.
words.ctx: The king was {capricious}: one day he rewarded his cook with gold, and the next, for no reason anyone could see, he banished him from the kitchen.

mn.cue: a goat on a whim: this way, then that
mn.text: The little goat leaps left, then right, then left again, for no reason at all: just a whim. Its leaping is {capricious}.

scene.alt: A goat leaps one way, then the other, for no reason at all.

words.ex: The {fickle} cat loved me on Monday and ignored me by Tuesday.
words.ctx: Fans can be {fickle}: they cheered the young pitcher all spring, then booed him the moment he lost two games in a row.

mn.cue: a FICKLE NICKEL: flips like a coin
mn.text: Ivy picks her best friend by flipping a nickel: heads it’s Zoe, tails it’s Lila, and tomorrow she flips again. Loyalty that flips like a coin is {fickle}.

scene.alt: A girl flips a coin to choose her best friend while two friends look confused.

words.ex: The old car’s {erratic} engine coughed, roared and then went silent.
words.ctx: Lin’s sleep became {erratic} during exam week: some nights she slept three hours, some nights eleven, and she never went to bed at the same time twice.
words.etym: From Latin erraticus, “wandering,” from errare, “to wander, to stray,” the root of error.

mn.text: The pet rat zigzags across the floor, left, right, back, around the sofa, so no one can guess where it will go next. Its path is {erratic}.

scene.alt: A pet rat zigzags across the floor while a man tries to follow it.

words.def: likely to change suddenly, often for the worse
words.ex: The {volatile} stock market rose sharply in the morning and fell by afternoon.
words.ctx: The mood at the meeting was {volatile}: one careless word, and the calm discussion could explode into shouting.
words.etym: From Latin volatilis, “flying,” from volare, “to fly”: a volatile liquid quickly flies off into the air.

mn.cue: VOL-atile: a VOLCANO ready to blow
mn.text: Dev’s science-fair volcano rumbles and fizzes, and no one knows when it will blow. Anything ready to erupt or change suddenly is {volatile}.

scene.alt: A model volcano fizzes and smokes on a table while two students jump back.

words.def: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
words.ex: The {mercurial} chef was laughing one minute and shouting the next.
words.ctx: Working for the {mercurial} director was exhausting: she praised a scene warmly in the morning and called the same scene a disaster that afternoon.
words.etym: From Latin mercurialis, “of Mercury,” the swift messenger of Roman myth; the quick, slippery liquid metal mercury carries the same name.

mn.text: Chef Victor laughs at a joke, roars at a dropped spoon, then hums happily, all in one minute. His moods slip and dart like quick, silvery mercury: he is {mercurial}.

scene.alt: A chef swings from laughing to shouting to humming while a boy watches, dizzy.

words.ex: In an {impulsive} moment, Jonah dyed his hair green the night before school photos.
words.ctx: Ivy’s purchase was {impulsive}: she saw the giant teddy bear at the checkout and bought it without a single thought about where it would fit in her tiny room.
words.etym: From Latin impulsus, “a push,” from impellere, “to push on”: im (on) + pellere (to drive).

mn.text: Ivy spots a giant teddy bear at the checkout and buys it in one heartbeat, without a thought about where it will fit. Her purchase is {impulsive}.

scene.alt: A girl hugs a giant teddy bear she bought on the spot while the cashier wonders where it will fit.

words.def: acting quickly and rashly, without thought
words.ex: The {impetuous} knight charged across the river without checking how deep it was.
words.ctx: Dev’s {impetuous} decision to quit the team after one bad game surprised everyone, and by the next morning he was asking the coach to let him back.
words.etym: From Latin impetuosus, from impetus, “a rush, an attack.”

mn.text: Dev races down the dock and leaps into the lake without checking how cold it is. Splash! Brrr! His headlong leap was {impetuous}.

scene.alt: A teen leaps headlong off the dock into a chilly lake without checking first.

words.ex: The crowd broke into {spontaneous} applause when the puppy crossed the finish line.
words.ctx: Nothing about the party was planned: it was {spontaneous}, starting when one neighbor brought out a guitar and others drifted over with snacks and folding chairs.
words.etym: From Latin sponte, “of one’s own accord, freely.”

mn.text: One neighbor starts strumming a guitar on her steps, and soon the whole street is dancing, with no plan at all. The party is {spontaneous}.

scene.alt: A neighbor plays guitar and others start dancing in the street, unplanned.

words.def: to waver back and forth between choices
words.ex: Kai {vacillated} between chocolate and vanilla until the shop closed.
words.ctx: For weeks Ada {vacillated} about the job offer: one day she was packing boxes for the move, and the next she was telling friends she would stay.
words.etym: From Latin vacillare, “to sway, to totter.”

mn.text: Kai stares at the menu: vanilla? chocolate? vanilla? He sways back and forth so long that the shop closes. To waver like that is to {vacillate}.

scene.alt: A boy wavers between a vanilla cone and a chocolate cone.

words.ex: The price of strawberries {fluctuates} with the seasons.
words.ctx: Desert temperatures {fluctuate} wildly: an afternoon can top 100 degrees, and the same night can drop close to freezing.
words.etym: From Latin fluctuare, “to move like a wave,” from fluctus, a wave.

mn.text: The little boat rides the waves up, down, up, down, never level for a moment. Things that rise and fall like waves {fluctuate}.

scene.alt: A little boat rocks up and down on the waves beside a bobbing duck.

after.cap: Who or what is changing, and how.

after.html: spontaneous is usually praise (a spontaneous laugh, a spontaneous party), while impulsive and impetuous usually warn: they mean acting before thinking. And vacillate is about indecision in a mind; fluctuate is about numbers and amounts going up and down.

items.q: Which word is most likely to be a compliment?
items.why: Spontaneous (natural, unplanned) is often praise. Impetuous, impulsive and erratic usually suggest rashness or unreliability.

items.q: Gas prices went up, then down, then up again all year. Prices…
items.why: Amounts that rise and fall fluctuate. Vacillate is for a person wavering between choices.

items.q: Unable to decide between the two colleges, Maya changed her mind every day for a month. She…
items.why: Wavering back and forth between choices is vacillating.

items.q: True or false: a fickle friend is loyal no matter what.
items.why: False. A fickle friend changes loyalties and feelings often.
